newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japanese shoppers take higher sales tax calmly.
newsitem.headline: Japanese shoppers take higher sales tax calmly.

text.p: Japanese consumers did some last-minute buying ahead of a Tuesday increase in the national sales tax, but there was no stampede to the stores and most people seemed to shrug off the higher tax burden.
The consumption tax rises to five percent from three percent at the beginning of the new fiscal year as part of an attempt to reduce the massive government budget deficit.
While the tax is still low by international standards, the financial drain will do little to help a faltering economy gain strength.
A short-term boost to the economy had been expected from shoppers trying to beat the higher prices, especially in big-ticket items such as automobiles and houses.
But stores said it turned into more of a boomlet.
Shops reported that sales were higher than usual in the last weekend before the tax rise but said extra staff easily coped with the mini-rush.
"The sales tax rise set off active weekend shopping," said a spokesman for Tokyo's Sogo department store, one of the country's largest.
"It was about 10 percent better than the same period last year and covered all items," he added.
A spokesman for Ito Yokado, a major supermarket chain, estimated weekend sales were up almost 20 percent.
"It's still active today. People are tending to buy air conditioners, TV sets, furniture and alcohol," the spokesman said.
However, unlike 1989 when the three percent sales tax was introduced, there were no signs of a stampede by shoppers to buy before prices went up.
"This time there has been no panic-buying. People acted much wiser," the Sogo spokesman said.
According to the Finance Ministry, the tax increase imposes extra costs of 67,000 yen ($540) a year on a four-member household with annual earnings of seven million yen ($56,400).
The figure set off a lively weekend debate in newspapers about how families should cope with the extra spending.
"As a compromise I have decided to go without alcoholic beverages one day a week. My wife will also stop purchasing a monthly magazine," Shosaku Ito said in a letter to the Daily Yomiuri.
Finance Minister Hiroshi Mitsuzuka promised last week the government will not consider raising the consumption tax again before 2005.
But Harikrishna Bhat, another newspaper letter writer, warned the public should beware of promises of no more rises.
"One thing is certain. If people keep quiet, this consumption tax disease will worsen in the coming years," he wrote.
There was no rush to beat the higher costs in one of the biggest expenses facing a new family -- a wedding.
Wedding planners said that couples were putting romance -- or possibly the lack of it -- ahead of economics.
"We haven't seen any panic weddings because of the higher costs," said a spokesman for the Keio Plaza Hotel, a popular location for marriage ceremonies.
"People don't tend to be stingy on such an occasion, so young couples don't seem to care about paying extra money if it's after April 1," he said.
